headline: Penang's 520% tourism surge: who counts the arrivals and who pays the rent
context: Malaysia's Middle East arrivals fell 40% in March 2026. Penang pivoted hard to China, India, and ASEAN: 161,599 Chinese tourists in nine months. George Town's heritage core has long depopulated.

changes.summary: Correction: In two cards, replaced unverified heritage-core figures (50,000 to 9,000 residents; 80% lost since 2008) with a statement that the core has long been losing residents.

Correction: the context still said George Town's heritage core "lost 80% of residents since UNESCO listing". The 8 Apr 2026 correction removed that unverifiable figure from the cards but missed the context.

Correction: We removed a line about named communities that no source supported, and other unsourced figures and claims, including 61 weekly flights and a missing carrying-capacity study. China's RM20.87 billion in 2024 visitor spending and the airport expansion to 12 million passengers now cite official and news sources.

cards.big: 520% more Chinese tourists landed in Penang, but the success story has a rent bill attached
cards.sub: The 520% surge uses a low 2023 base of 26,056. George Town's historic core has long depopulated.

cards.big: Visitors from China spent RM20.87B in Malaysia in 2024, second only to Singapore. The 'low-value tourist' claim doesn't survive the data.
cards.sub: That is about RM5,600 per visitor from China, twice the RM2,800 average for all visitors. Tourism Malaysia's 2024 figures give no Penang split.

cards.big: A 2017 study dates George Town's gentrification to the 1997 end of rent control, and says the 2008 UNESCO listing sped it up.
cards.sub: Its authors warn that gentrification can displace long-term residents and erode local culture.

cards.big: Penang is building for more arrivals: its airport expansion lifts capacity from 6.5 million to 12 million passengers a year by June 2028.
cards.sub: Malaysia Airports' group managing director confirmed the June 2028 target in July 2025.

cards.big: This isn't about Chinese tourists versus heritage. It's about who profits from growth and who pays rent.
Penang needs a public dashboard tracking residents, rents, and local retention, not just arrivals
